section.title: The Vision of the Ram and the Goat
section.sectionRationale: The book returns to Hebrew for a vision that narrows the focus from all history to a particular crisis. A ram (Media-Persia) is shattered by a goat (Greece), whose great horn breaks into four, and from one of them rises a little horn that attacks the sanctuary, halts the daily sacrifice, and defies the Prince of the host, until it is broken by no human hand. Gabriel interprets it as a warning of a coming persecutor and a promise that the sanctuary will be restored.
section.thesis: God shows Daniel the named empires to come, Media-Persia and Greece, and a defiant king who will trample the sanctuary and halt worship for an appointed span, yet the vision fixes a limit to the desolation and promises that the sanctuary will be restored and the persecutor broken, not by human hands but by God.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the ram and the goat and the breaking of the great horn; the little horn that attacks the sanctuary and the promised restoration; Gabriel comes to interpret; and the named kingdoms, Media-Persia and Greece, and the insolent king broken by no human hand.

verses.text: In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar, a vision appeared to me, Daniel, subsequent to the one that had appeared to me earlier.
And in the vision I saw myself in the citadel of Susa, in the province of Elam. I saw in the vision that I was beside the Ulai Canal.
Then I lifted up my eyes and saw a ram with two horns standing beside the canal. The horns were long, but one was longer than the other, and the longer one grew up later.
I saw the ram charging toward the west and the north and the south. No animal could stand against him, and there was no deliverance from his power. He did as he pleased and became great.
As I was contemplating all this, suddenly a goat with a prominent horn between his eyes came out of the west, crossing the surface of the entire earth without touching the ground.
He came toward the two-horned ram I had seen standing beside the canal and rushed at him with furious power.

I saw him approach the ram in a rage against him, and he struck the ram and shattered his two horns. The ram was powerless to stand against him, and the goat threw him to the ground and trampled him, and no one could deliver the ram from his power.
Thus the goat became very great, but at the height of his power, his large horn was broken off, and four prominent horns came up in its place, pointing toward the four winds of heaven.

units.label: The little horn against the sanctuary

verses.text: From one of these horns a little horn emerged and grew extensively toward the south and the east and toward the Beautiful Land.
It grew as high as the host of heaven, and it cast down some of the host and some of the stars to the earth and trampled them.
It magnified itself, even to the {{sar|Prince}} of the host; it removed His {{tamid|daily sacrifice}} and overthrew the place of His sanctuary.
And in the rebellion, the host and the daily sacrifice were given over to the horn, and it flung truth to the ground and prospered in whatever it did.

Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one said to him, “How long until the fulfillment of the vision of the daily sacrifice, the rebellion that causes desolation, and the surrender of the sanctuary and of the host to be trampled?”
He said to me, “It will take 2,300 evenings and mornings; then the {{qodesh|sanctuary}} will be properly restored.”

units.label: Gabriel comes to interpret
units.note: the vision concerns the time of the end

verses.text: While I, Daniel, was watching the vision and trying to understand it, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man.
And I heard the voice of a man calling from between the banks of the Ulai: “Gabriel, explain the vision to this man.”
As he came near to where I stood, I was terrified and fell facedown. “Son of man,” he said to me, “understand that the vision concerns the {{qets|time of the end}}.”
While he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep, with my face to the ground. Then he touched me, helped me to my feet,
and said, “Behold, I will make known to you what will happen in the latter time of wrath, because it concerns the appointed time of the end.

units.label: The named kingdoms and the insolent king
units.note: broken, but not by human hands

verses.text: The two-horned ram that you saw represents the kings of Media and Persia.
The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece, and the large horn between his eyes is the first king.
The four horns that replaced the broken one represent four kingdoms that will rise from that nation but will not have the same power.
In the latter part of their reign, when the rebellion has reached its full measure, an insolent king, skilled in intrigue, will come to the throne.
His power will be great, but it will not be his own. He will cause terrible destruction and succeed in whatever he does. He will destroy the mighty men along with the holy people.

Through his craft and by his hand, he will cause deceit to prosper, and in his own mind he will make himself great. In a time of peace he will destroy many, and he will even stand against the Prince of princes. Yet he will be broken off, but not by human hands.
The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been spoken is true. Now you must seal up the vision, for it concerns the distant future.”
I, Daniel, was exhausted and lay ill for days. Then I got up and went about the king's business. I was confounded by the vision; it was beyond understanding.

sar.gloss: A prince, commander, or chief. The little horn exalts itself even against the Prince of the host and the Prince of princes, that is, against God Himself or His anointed leader. The word sets the whole conflict in perspective: an arrogant human power dares to challenge the true Prince, and loses.

tamid.gloss: The regular, continual burnt offering, the daily sacrifice offered morning and evening in the temple. The persecutor's great crime is to remove the tamid, cutting off the appointed worship of God. Its restoration signals that God will not let His worship be silenced forever.

qodesh.gloss: Holiness, a holy place, the sanctuary. The horn tramples and defiles the qodesh, but the vision promises that the sanctuary will be properly restored, or set right. God's holy dwelling and worship, though desecrated for a season, will be cleansed and vindicated.

qets.gloss: An end, appointed conclusion. Gabriel says the vision concerns the time of the qets, the appointed end. The word signals that the persecution has a fixed terminus set by God; evil is never open-ended but runs to a boundary God has already drawn.

basic.context: Daniel sees a two-horned ram trampling all before it, then a swift goat with one great horn that shatters the ram. The goat's horn breaks and becomes four, and from one of them a little horn rises that grows toward God's land, attacks the sanctuary, stops the daily sacrifice, and defies the Prince of the host. A heavenly voice fixes a limit to the desecration, after which the sanctuary will be restored. The angel Gabriel explains: the ram is Media-Persia, the goat is Greece, and the little horn is a coming insolent king who will be broken by no human hand.
basic.hermeneutics: Unusually, this vision is largely interpreted for us: Gabriel names the empires. The little horn corresponds closely to Antiochus IV, who desecrated the temple and banned the sacrifices in the second century BC, and many also see in him a pattern of the final antichrist. The vision is meant to prepare God's people for a fierce but limited persecution, assuring them the sanctuary will be cleansed and the tyrant destroyed by God.
basic.originalLanguages: The horn attacks the tamid, the daily sacrifice, and defiles the qodesh, the sanctuary, exalting itself against the sar, the Prince of the host. But Gabriel says the vision concerns the qets, the appointed end: the desolation has a fixed limit, after which the sanctuary is restored.
basic.typology: The desecration of the sanctuary and the halting of the sacrifice, followed by cleansing and restoration, foreshadow the greater pattern in Christ, whose body is the true temple, torn down and raised, and who cleanses and secures a worship that can never finally be stopped. The tyrant broken by no human hand points to the defeat of every God-defying power by God alone.
basic.christ: The little horn stands against the Prince of princes, but is shattered without a human hand, by God's own power. This anticipates Christ's victory over every proud enemy. Christ is the true Prince and the true sanctuary; His worship cannot be silenced, and the enemies who assault His people will be broken not by human strength but by the Lord Himself.
basic.god: God is the sovereign who names empires before they rise and sets a strict boundary to the worst persecutions. Even when His sanctuary is defiled and His worship halted, He has already fixed the day of restoration. He alone breaks the tyrant, and He assures His people that evil is measured and limited.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 11 revisits this Greek king in detail. First and second Maccabees record the desecration under Antiochus and the temple's cleansing. And Jesus in Matthew 24 speaks of an abomination of desolation, drawing on Daniel's imagery.
basic.oneStory: God pulls back the curtain on the specific empires His exiled people will face and warns of a bitter persecution to come, yet He fixes its limit and promises the sanctuary will be cleansed. The pattern of desecration and restoration finds its fullness in Christ, the true temple, and in the God who breaks every proud enemy by His own hand and secures a worship that endures forever.

context.literary:
With chapter 8 the language of the book changes from Aramaic back to Hebrew, and the book's mode changes with it. Chapters 2 to 7 are the book's wide-angle view of the nations, in the language of the empire. Chapters 8 to 12 return to Hebrew, the language of Israel, and narrow the focus to what the empires will do to God's own people and their sanctuary. The vision is also the first one in the book to be explained in full by a named angel.

The chapter has the shape of a vision followed by an interpretation, and a closing note of exhaustion. Verses 1 to 14 give the vision in three movements: the ram, verses 3 and 4; the goat, verses 5 to 8; and the little horn, verses 9 to 12, which is followed by a heavenly conversation in verses 13 and 14. Verses 15 to 26 interpret it, with Gabriel naming each empire in verses 20 to 22 and then dwelling on the king in verses 23 to 25. Verse 27 closes with Daniel ill, and then at work.

The vision is built on a descending staircase of power. The ram does 'as he pleased and became great,' verse 4. The goat is greater, 'very great,' verse 8, and the horn grows 'as high as the host of heaven,' verse 10. Each is then broken. The ram's horns are shattered, the goat's large horn is broken at its height, and the last horn is 'broken off, but not by human hands,' verse 25. The verb for breaking marks the fall of each, and the chain of broken horns carries the point.

Another thread is the verb of understanding. Daniel contemplates in verse 5, seeks to understand in verse 15, is told to give understanding in verse 16 and to understand in verse 17, and at the end is 'confounded', and there was no one to explain it, verse 27. The chapter is about the struggle to understand what God is doing when the sanctuary falls.
context.historical:
Daniel dates the vision to the third year of Belshazzar, about 551 BC, and places himself in the citadel of Susa, in Elam, beside the Ulai Canal, verse 2. Susa was not yet the Persian capital, and in the vision he may be there in the spirit and not in the body. It later became one of the winter capitals of the Persian kings, the place where Esther and Nehemiah are set, Esther 1:2 and Nehemiah 1:1. The vision therefore looks from the middle of Babylon's decline toward the empire that will replace it.

The ram with two horns, one longer and later-growing, fits the Medo-Persian alliance in which the Persian partner overtook the Median, and the charge to the west, north and south matches the Persian conquests in Asia Minor, Mesopotamia and Egypt. The goat from the west that crosses the earth 'without touching the ground' is Alexander of Macedon, whose armies swept through the Persian empire in about ten years, from 334 to 323 BC. Gabriel names it plainly, and the BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew of verse 21 says 'Javan,' the ancient name for Greece. Alexander died young at the height of his power, and his empire was divided by his generals into four main kingdoms, as the four horns of verse 8 describe.

The little horn comes from one of those successor kingdoms. Antiochus IV Epiphanes ruled the Seleucid Empire from 175 BC. He came to the throne by intrigue, tried to impose Greek ways on his Jewish subjects, and in 167 BC banned the practice of Judaism, stopped the daily offering and set up a pagan altar in the temple, 1 Maccabees 1. The temple was rededicated in 164 BC after the Maccabean revolt, three years later, an event remembered in the Feast of Dedication, John 10:22. Antiochus himself died not long after, of an illness, away from the battlefield.

For the exiles who first received the book, the vision was a promise that a long sequence of powers was already known to God.
context.canonical:
The vision is not an isolated oddity but part of a sustained treatment of the same period. Daniel 11 gives a far fuller account of the clash between the kings of the north and south, with an unmistakable picture of a contemptible king who will 'desecrate the temple fortress' and 'abolish the daily sacrifice,' Daniel 11:31. Daniel 9:27 and 12:11 speak in the same terms of a desolating abomination and the end of the sacrifice. The visions of chapters 2, 7 and 8 therefore share one outline: the nations in sequence, a defiant power at the end, and a kingdom that God sets up.

The Gospels pick up that language. Jesus warns His disciples, 'So when you see standing in the holy place "the abomination of desolation," described by the prophet Daniel,' and adds 'let the reader understand,' Matthew 24:15. His words about Jerusalem being 'trodden down by the Gentiles' in Luke 21:24 echo the trampling of the sanctuary and host in Daniel 8:13. Paul's picture of a lawless one who sits in the temple of God, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4, and Revelation's 42 months in which the nations trample the holy city, Revelation 11:2, belong to the same trajectory.

The chapter also stands behind later Jewish history. The Feast of Dedication that Jesus attended in the temple courts in winter, John 10:22 to 23, commemorates the cleansing that followed Antiochus's desecration, and the endurance of the faithful in the Maccabean period is thought by many to lie behind Hebrews 11:35 to 38. Gabriel, who appears here for the first time by name, verse 16, is the same angel who stands before God and comes to Zechariah and to Mary, Luke 1:19 and 1:26 to 33."

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Daniel writes to people who will see the sanctuary threatened and who need to know, before it happens, that God has seen it. The vision gives them an advance copy of the sequence: the ram, the goat, the horn that rises from the goat. The point of an advance copy is that when it comes true, they will know it was not a surprise to God. The empires have names in heaven before they have armies on earth.

He also wants them to be ready for a persecution that attacks worship itself. The horn does not merely conquer; it halts the daily sacrifice, throws down the place of the sanctuary and 'flung truth to the ground,' verse 12. The faithful will find that the thing they live by has been forbidden. The author's word to them is that the attack is real, that the host and the sanctuary are 'trampled,' and that God has already fixed its length.

And he wants them to see that the oppressor's power is borrowed. The horn's power 'will be great, but it will not be his own,' verse 24, which means that its strength comes by permission. He will be broken, and not by an army. The expected response to such a vision is endurance and patience. The author does not call the people to arms. He tells them that the vision is true, that it concerns a distant time, and that they should seal it up, verse 26, and trust the God who has written the timetable.

The chapter also ends on a personal note. Daniel is ill for days, and then he goes back to the king's business, verse 27. The author thus models a response to terrifying revelation: be honest about the weight of it, and then return to ordinary faithfulness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what Daniel saw and what Gabriel said. It does not prescribe a method for matching beasts to news, and it does not authorise the setting of dates. The number 2,300 is a number in a vision, and the angel does not give a calendar on which to calculate it. Daniel himself, who received the vision, 'was confounded' and did not understand it, verse 27, and the reader should be slow to claim more.

What the chapter gives as a model is its pattern. When powerful and clever rulers use religion as a weapon and the worship of God is outlawed, the response of the faithful is to endure and to trust God's word that the time is limited. The people who are cast down, the host and the stars, are not abandoned; they are named and remembered. The final act belongs to God, who breaks the tyrant 'not by human hands.'

The chapter also warns against a cheap reading. The horn does not succeed because God is weak. 'In the rebellion, the host and the daily sacrifice were given over to the horn,' verse 12, and the passive leaves God as the unnamed giver, which means He permits it. The passage describes a permitted evil. It does not say that every setback of the church is God's judgment, or that every ruler who opposes believers is the little horn.

debates.question: Is the little horn only Antiochus IV, or also a picture of the final antichrist?

views.label: Primarily Antiochus IV Epiphanes
views.case: The details fit Antiochus with remarkable precision: rising from the Greek successor kingdoms, attacking the Beautiful Land, halting the daily sacrifice, desecrating the temple, and dying suddenly by no human hand; the vision's 2,300 evenings and mornings roughly span his desecration to the temple's rededication.

views.label: Antiochus as a type of a greater end-time enemy
views.case: Gabriel repeatedly ties the vision to the time of the end and the appointed end, and Jesus later speaks of an abomination of desolation as still future; so many read Antiochus as a real historical fulfillment that also prefigures a final antichrist who will be destroyed at Christ's coming.

debates.bearing: Either way the assurance is the same: however far a defiant power goes in desecrating what is holy and crushing God's people, its time is fixed, the sanctuary will be restored, and God Himself will break it.

debates.question: How long are the 2,300 evenings and mornings?

views.label: 2,300 days, about six and a half years
views.case: The phrase is read as 2,300 full days, with evening and morning together as one day, as in Genesis 1:5. On this view the span begins before the open persecution of 167 BC and runs to the cleansing of the temple, or it is a round figure for a long season of trouble.

views.label: 1,150 days, or 2,300 offerings
views.case: The daily sacrifice was offered each morning and each evening, Exodus 29:38-42, so 2,300 evenings and mornings counts 2,300 separate offerings, which makes 1,150 days, a little over three years. That agrees with the interval between the desecration in 167 BC and the rededication in 164 BC. It also fits Daniel 12:11, which gives 1,290 days for a related period.

debates.bearing: The text means to give a fixed limit to the desolation, and each reading keeps that. It is a matter on which an honest reader should hold the arithmetic loosely and hold the promise firmly: it ends and the sanctuary is made right.

debates.question: Who is the Prince of the host and the Prince of princes?

views.label: God Himself
views.case: The horn magnifies itself 'even to the Prince of the host,' verse 11, and stands against the 'Prince of princes,' verse 25. The attacks on His sanctuary and daily sacrifice make the target God, and 'Prince of princes' is a superlative that is parallel to 'God of gods,' Daniel 11:36. Joshua 5:14 uses the same word for the Commander of the LORD's army.

views.label: An angelic commander, such as Michael
views.case: The host in verse 10 is the host of heaven, and Daniel elsewhere calls Michael 'your prince,' Daniel 10:21, and 'one of the chief princes,' Daniel 10:13. The Prince of the host might then be the angel who leads God's people, and the attack on him a way of saying that the horn assaulted the heavenly forces.

debates.bearing: The language of sacrifice and sanctuary points to God as the one attacked. Christian readers have seen in the title the one who is the Lord of lords, and the Lamb who overcomes the horn's successors, Revelation 17:14. In either case the pride of the horn rises to the highest level and is met by the highest answer.

study.originalLanguages:
The first thing to notice is the verb of breaking. In verse 7 the goat 'shattered' the ram's two horns, in verse 8 the large horn was 'broken off,' and in verse 25 the little horn 'will be broken off,' all from one Hebrew root. The three empires meet the same end by the same verb, which is a quiet way of saying that each is a story of power broken by something greater. The last use differs in one point only: the little horn is broken 'not by human hands,' a phrase that in Hebrew means literally without a hand.

That phrase connects the chapter with Daniel 2:45, where the stone that destroys the statue is 'cut out of the mountain without human hands.' The Aramaic and Hebrew phrases differ, but the idea is the same, a defeat that comes from God and not from an army. The horn, who gets his power by his own hand and craft, verse 25, is undone by a hand that is not his.

The second is the verb that closes the heavenly answer in verse 14. The sanctuary 'will be properly restored.' The Hebrew verb is built on the root for righteousness and justice, in a form that can mean to be put right, to be vindicated. It is a different word from the common words for cleansing or rebuilding. The sanctuary is not only cleaned of what was done to it, but declared in the right, and its worship justified. The wrong that was done is answered by God's own verdict.

Third, the phrase 'the Beautiful Land' in verse 9 renders a Hebrew word for beauty or splendour, used of the land of Israel in Daniel 11:16 and 11:41, and in Ezekiel 20:6 of the land as 'the glory of all lands.' The horn grows toward the land God's people were given as an inheritance and which He called glorious.

Fourth, the phrase 'evenings and mornings' in verses 14 and 26 uses the pattern of Genesis 1: 'there was evening, and there was morning,' Genesis 1:5. The creation days were counted in this way. In Daniel it is the daily offering that is counted, so the language of the first creation week frames the interruption of Israel's daily worship. The vision of verse 26 is also called 'the vision of the evenings and the mornings,' as though the whole thing were measured out by the rhythm of the sacrifice.

Fifth, the angel addresses Daniel as 'son of man,' verse 17. The Hebrew phrase is the one that God uses constantly to address Ezekiel, for example Ezekiel 2:1, and it means a mortal human being. In chapter 7 an Aramaic phrase of nearly the same shape described the figure who approached the Ancient of Days. Here the same phrase marks Daniel as a frail man who has fallen on his face. The use of the phrase for Daniel and the one in chapter 7 differ in what they stress: one the weakness of a human being, the other the glory given to One who is truly human.

Sixth, the description of the king in verse 23 as 'insolent' is literally 'hard of face,' a person who cannot be embarrassed or turned back, and 'skilled in intrigue' translates a phrase that suggests a master of riddles and schemes. The king is a skilled deceiver whose chief weapon is deceit, verse 25, which agrees with the horn that 'flung truth to the ground,' verse 12.

Finally, the 'latter time of wrath,' verse 19, uses the word for indignation. The wrath is not primarily the king's. It is God's own indignation at a people's sin, and the king is the tool by which it is poured out. The vision is therefore about more than a villain: God's anger is real, and it is also limited by an appointed end.

typology.type: The desecrated and restored sanctuary, Daniel 8:11-14
typology.fulfillment: The sanctuary is thrown down and the daily offering is taken away, and then God declares that it will be put right. The Maccabean cleansing of 164 BC was a real restoration, remembered at the Feast of Dedication, John 10:22-23. But Jesus points beyond the stone temple. When He cleansed the temple in John 2:13-17 and spoke of 'the temple of His body,' John 2:21, He showed Himself as the true sanctuary that is torn down and raised. Hebrews says He entered 'the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands,' Hebrews 9:11. The type falls short because the rededicated temple could be, and was, defiled again, but the sanctuary in Christ cannot be.

The horn stops the daily offering of two lambs, morning and evening, that Exodus 29:38-42 required. What the persecutor could not know was that those daily offerings were never able to finish the work. Hebrews 10:11-14 says that every priest stands daily to offer the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins, but Christ offered 'for all time one sacrifice for sins' and sat down. The offering the horn interrupted was a shadow. The sacrifice of Christ cannot be halted, repeated or taken away. The type is a real picture of how worship is threatened, and a limited one, since its own work was always provisional.

typology.type: The little horn who stands against the Prince of princes, Daniel 8:23-25
typology.fulfillment: A king skilled in deceit stands against the highest Prince and is broken by no human hand. The pattern recurs in the New Testament with larger scope. Paul describes a lawless one whom the Lord Jesus will 'slay with the breath of His mouth,' 2 Thessalonians 2:8, and Revelation 19:19 to 21 shows the beast and the kings of the earth gathered against the rider on the horse and overthrown. Revelation 17:14 says the Lamb triumphs over those who make war against Him because He is 'Lord of lords and King of kings.' Antiochus is a real fulfilment in his time and a pattern for the last enemy, and Jesus Himself uses Daniel's language of desolation for what is still to come, Matthew 24:15.

typology.type: The stars cast down and trampled, Daniel 8:10
typology.fulfillment: The horn casts some of the host and some of the stars to the earth and tramples them. Verse 24 tells us the horn will 'destroy the mighty men along with the holy people,' so the stars appear to be God's people, and Daniel 12:3 says that those who lead many to righteousness 'will shine like the stars forever and ever.' The faithful who are trampled in the vision are promised to shine. In Christ this takes its fullest form: the One who was trampled and killed is the firstborn from the dead, and His people share His glory, Romans 8:17. The type is a pattern of suffering followed by vindication, and its limit is that Daniel does not say how the stars will be raised.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the Prince of princes. The horn magnifies itself even against the Prince of the host and stands against the Prince of princes, and the Bible has only one way of speaking about a Prince above all princes. Isaiah calls the promised Son 'Prince of Peace,' Isaiah 9:6, and Revelation names the Lamb 'Lord of lords and King of kings,' Revelation 17:14. Whatever the vision first meant, the New Testament places the One who has the highest title where the attack of the horn falls. The Commander of the LORD's army who appeared to Joshua, Joshua 5:14, who is the same title in Hebrew, is part of this background, and Christian readers have heard in it a hint of the Son.

It leads to Christ through the sanctuary. The vision is about a temple under assault, and the verdict that it will be put right. Jesus took the temple language to Himself. He cleansed the temple courts and said that He would raise 'the temple of His body' in three days, John 2:19-21. He sat in the temple at the Feast of Dedication, the very festival that remembered the cleansing after Antiochus, John 10:22 to 23, and said there that He and the Father are one. The One who is greater than the temple walked in its courts at the very festival that celebrated its restoration. Hebrews adds that He passed through the greater tabernacle, not made by hands, and entered once for all, Hebrews 9:11 to 12.

It leads to Christ through the sacrifice. The horn halts the daily offering, and the New Testament says the offering was always pointing past itself, to the one sacrifice that was made for all time, Hebrews 10:11 to 14. The enemy's blow at the sacrifice cannot touch the sacrifice that matters.

It leads to Christ through the way the horn falls. 'Broken off, but not by human hands,' recalls the stone cut out without hands in Daniel 2:45, and the New Testament shows that the lawless one will be slain by the breath of the Lord's mouth, 2 Thessalonians 2:8. Where the horn's whole strategy was craft and his own hand, his end is by the word of a King he has defied.

And it leads to Christ through Gabriel. The angel who explains the vision of the kingdoms that come and go is the one who appears again in the Gospel of Luke to tell Mary that her son will receive the throne of David and that 'His kingdom will never end,' Luke 1:31 to 33. The messenger who taught Daniel that the empires will be broken is sent to announce the One to whom the kingdom belongs.

The usual caution holds. The ram and the goat are not codes for the Lord, and the numbers are not predictions of the date of the cross. Gabriel himself interprets the vision as a matter of empires and a persecutor. The link to Christ is made by the New Testament's use of this chapter and by the larger pattern of a Prince who is attacked and a sanctuary that is vindicated.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He is the author of history's order. Gabriel names the powers and their sequence before any of them rise, and says that the ram is Media and Persia and the goat is Greece. A reader who has just seen the empires as huge and terrifying learns that their schedule is in the hands of Someone else. Isaiah 46:10 makes the same claim about the God who declares the end from the beginning, and Daniel 8 is a particular case of it.

He is sovereign over evil without being its author. The horn does what it does because 'the host and the daily sacrifice were given over to the horn,' verse 12. Evil is permitted for a time. Yet the same verses name its guilt: the horn magnifies itself against the Prince, flings truth to the ground and prospers. The text refuses both easy answers. God is not made the cause of the horn's pride, and the horn is not outside God's governance.

He is the God who measures. The question 'How long?' in verse 13 is the question of the whole Bible, and the answer is a number. The persecution is not endless. It has a beginning and an end that have been fixed, and the sanctuary will be put right. A God who gives numbers to suffering is not indifferent to it. He sets limits on how far the horn may go.

He is a God who hears the questions of heaven. One holy one asks another how long, and it is not Daniel who asks. The angels are concerned for the sanctuary. The people of God are not the only ones who care about what is happening to it, and God's court is attentive.

He is a God of truth. The horn throws truth to the ground; God's answer is to make it stand. The angel calls the vision 'true,' verse 26, though much of it was beyond Daniel to understand. God does not ask for faith in a message that is vague. He asks Daniel to seal it up, because it concerns a future that He alone governs.

He is a God who is gentle with a frightened prophet. When Daniel falls on his face, the angel touches him and helps him to his feet, verse 18. The mighty God who explains the rise and fall of nations is the one who sends a messenger to lift a terrified man.

He is a God who breaks the proud without human help. 'Not by human hands' is the strongest statement of God's sole sufficiency. He needs no army, and He does not share the glory.

For worship, the chapter calls us to a patient trust. We are not told the date, and we are not told how all the pieces fit. We are told that the vision is true, that evil is measured, that the sanctuary will be made right, and that the God who knows the end is the one who holds the pen.

crossReferences.note: The stone is cut out of the mountain without human hands and shatters the statue. Daniel 8:25 says that the king will be broken 'not by human hands,' so the end of the empire and the end of its last tyrant are both the work of God alone.

The long vision of Daniel 11 returns to this king, saying that his forces will desecrate the temple fortress, abolish the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination of desolation. It fills out the picture that Daniel 8:9 to 14 gives in outline.

Those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever. In Daniel 8:10 the horn casts down some of the stars and tramples them, so the later promise answers the earlier sorrow: the faithful who were trampled are the ones who will shine.

Jesus tells His disciples that when they see the abomination of desolation, described by the prophet Daniel, they are to understand. He speaks of Daniel's desecration as a pattern for what is coming, which supports reading Antiochus as both a historical fulfilment and a type.

Jerusalem 'will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.' The trampling of the sanctuary and host in Daniel 8:13 is taken up in this word of Jesus, with the same note of a limited time that ends when God says it ends.

The lawless one will be slain by the Lord Jesus with the breath of His mouth. This echoes the king in Daniel 8:25 who is broken without human hands, and shows that Christ's victory over the last enemy is by a word and not by a battle.

The Feast of Dedication, held in winter, celebrates the restoration of the temple after Antiochus. Jesus walks in the temple courts at that festival, so that the One who is the true sanctuary stands within the shadow of the cleansing that Daniel 8:14 promised.

Priests offered the same sacrifices day after day, but Christ offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down. The daily offering that the horn takes away in Daniel 8:11 was never able to finish the work, and the permanent answer is the one offering of Christ.

The figure who meets Joshua introduces himself as Commander of the LORD's army, and Joshua falls facedown in reverence. The title is the same as 'Prince of the host' in Daniel 8:11, which suggests that the horn's pride was set against the God who leads heaven's armies.

The kings who make war against the Lamb are overcome because He is Lord of lords and King of kings. The title answers the horn's challenge to the 'Prince of princes' in Daniel 8:25, and carries it to its end.

Gabriel, who explained Daniel's vision, comes to Mary and says that her son will receive the throne of David, and that His kingdom will never end. The angel who told Daniel that empires would be broken is sent to announce the King whose kingdom outlasts them all.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers a question that grew out of the exile: what will become of the sanctuary and the worship of God in a world run by empires that have no regard for either? From the Garden, where God's presence was the centre of life, to the tabernacle, to Solomon's temple, the Bible has been the story of a God who makes His dwelling among His people. Genesis 3 closed the garden, and every sanctuary since has been a partial return. When Daniel sees the sanctuary thrown down, he is seeing the loss of the thing that held the story together.

The vision answers that loss with two things. The first is that the powers who threaten the sanctuary are known, numbered and limited. The empires that will trample it have names, and the persecution has a length. The second is that the sanctuary will be put right. These are the same two things that the whole Bible will say about the presence of God: that no power can finally remove it, and that God Himself will restore what is spoiled.

What happened in 167 BC was a dress rehearsal for a longer history. The pattern of a ruler who sets himself against God and God's people, who stops worship and compels idolatry, and who is broken in the end by God, repeats in the New Testament in the figure of the lawless one and the beast. And the pattern of a sanctuary that is cleansed in answer is fulfilled in Christ, who is Himself the temple, who offered the one sacrifice that cannot be halted and who is now at the right hand of God.

The chapter also stands in the long line of the 'How long?' of the Psalms and the prophets. The question asked by the holy ones in verse 13 is the question the martyrs ask in Revelation 6:10, and the answer is the same: a limit has been set. The suffering of the people of God is not meaningless, and not endless.

The story ends in a city with no temple, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. There the daily sacrifice is no longer needed because the one sacrifice has been made, and there is no horn to cast truth to the ground. The people who were trampled stand in the light of God's face, and the sanctuary that Daniel saw thrown down is replaced by the dwelling of God with humanity.

quiz.q: What did Gabriel say the ram and the goat represent?

options.text: The ram is the kings of Media and Persia; the goat is the king of Greece.
options.note: Daniel 8:20-21 gives the explicit interpretation.

options.text: The ram is Babylon; the goat is Rome.
options.note: Gabriel names Media-Persia and Greece, not Babylon and Rome.

options.text: Two rival tribes of Israel.
options.note: They picture Gentile empires, not tribes of Israel.

options.text: Two false prophets.
options.note: They are kingdoms, expressly named by Gabriel.

quiz.q: What was the little horn's chief offense?

options.text: It attacked the sanctuary, removed the daily sacrifice, and exalted itself against the Prince of the host.
options.note: Daniel 8:11-12 centers the horn's crime on defiling worship and defying God.

options.text: It merely expanded its territory peacefully.
options.note: It did grow, but its defining sin was assaulting God's sanctuary and worship.

options.text: It built a rival temple to the true God.
options.note: It desecrated the existing sanctuary and stopped the sacrifice, not built a rival one.

options.text: It freed the Jewish exiles.
options.note: The opposite; it persecuted the holy people.

quiz.q: What did the heavenly voice promise about the sanctuary?

options.text: After an appointed span, it would be properly restored.
options.note: Daniel 8:14 fixes a limit and promises restoration.

options.text: It would be destroyed and never rebuilt.
options.note: The promise is restoration, not permanent ruin.

options.text: It would be moved to Babylon.
options.note: The sanctuary would be restored, not relocated.

options.text: It would remain defiled forever.
options.note: The desecration is limited; the sanctuary will be set right.

quiz.q: How would the insolent king finally meet his end?

options.text: He would be broken, but not by human hands, that is, by God Himself.
options.note: Daniel 8:25 stresses his destruction is God's direct act.

options.text: He would be defeated in a great battle by Israel's army.
options.note: The text says he is broken by no human hand, not by an army.

options.text: He would repent and turn to God.
options.note: He is broken in judgment, with no note of repentance.

options.text: He would rule forever.
options.note: His power is broken by God; it does not last.

quiz.q: How does this vision point us toward Christ?

options.text: The desecrated sanctuary is restored and the tyrant broken by God, pointing to Christ the true temple and the enemy destroyed by the Lord.
options.note: The pattern is fulfilled in Christ and God's defeat of every proud power, John 2:21 and 2 Thessalonians 2:8.

options.text: It teaches that armies always win God's battles.
options.note: The point is the opposite; the enemy is broken by no human hand.

options.text: It shows the temple in Jerusalem will never be touched.
options.note: The sanctuary is desecrated for a time, then restored; it is not untouchable.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The restored sanctuary and God-wrought victory point to Christ.

questions: The horn's great aim was to silence the worship of God. Where do you see pressures today that try to crowd out or shut down worship, and how do you keep worship central?
God fixed a limit to the desolation before it even began. How does knowing that hard seasons have a God-set boundary help you endure them?
The tyrant was broken by no human hand. Where are you tempted to rely on your own strength for a battle that only God can win?
Daniel was left exhausted and confounded by a vision he could not fully grasp. How do you hold on to trust when God's plans are beyond your understanding?
The promise was that the sanctuary would be restored. How does the certainty that God will finally set all things right encourage you in the middle of what is still broken?

translationNotes.note: The Beautiful Land is the land of Israel; the little horn's growth toward it marks its assault on God's people and their worship.
In the rebellion may also be rendered on account of transgression; the desolation is bound up with sin and defiance against God.
The 2,300 evenings and mornings is a fixed span, often linked to the period of Antiochus IV's desecration until the temple's cleansing; the point is a God-set limit.
Greece renders the Hebrew Javan; the great horn matches Alexander the Great, whose empire divided into four after his death.
